lessonTitle: Receptor Theory: Agonists, Antagonists and Receptor Families

blocks.text: A man is found unresponsive with slow shallow breathing and pinpoint pupils. A single injection of naloxone and within a minute or two he is breathing normally and waking up. Naloxone does nothing on its own in someone who has taken no opioid; it works only because it sits on the same receptors as the opioid and blocks them. How a drug binds, and what it does once bound, is the core of receptor theory.

blocks.markdown: A **receptor** is a macromolecule, usually a protein, to which a drug (ligand) binds to produce an effect. Two properties of a ligand matter: **affinity**, how tightly it binds, and **intrinsic efficacy** (intrinsic activity), how well the bound ligand activates the receptor. Drugs that bind and activate are **agonists**; drugs that bind without activating are **antagonists**.

blocks.title: Types of ligand
blocks.text: A full agonist produces the maximum response of the system. A partial agonist binds and activates but produces a submaximal response even when all receptors are occupied. A neutral (competitive) antagonist binds with affinity but no efficacy and blocks agonists. An inverse agonist binds the same receptor but reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below the resting level, producing an effect opposite to an agonist.

blocks.caption: Classes of ligand compared.
rows: Morphine at mu opioid receptors; isoprenaline at beta receptors
Many second-generation H1 antihistamines (for example cetirizine)

blocks.title: Classifying ligands from experimental data
blocks.prompt: On a tissue with a maximal response of 100 units: drug A gives 100 units; drug B gives a maximum of 40 units; drug C gives no response alone but shifts A's curve to the right; drug D, in a system with some baseline activity of 20 units, lowers the response to 5 units. Classify each drug.

steps.text: Drug A produces the full maximal response, so it is a full agonist.
Drug B produces only 40 units even at saturating concentration, so it is a partial agonist (affinity but intermediate efficacy).
Drug C has no effect by itself but reduces the effect of A, so it is an antagonist; a rightward shift indicates competition for the same site.
Drug D reduces activity below baseline, which a neutral antagonist could not do, so it is an inverse agonist.

blocks.answer: A full agonist; B partial agonist; C competitive antagonist; D inverse agonist

blocks.markdown: **Competitive antagonism.** A competitive antagonist binds reversibly to the same site as the agonist. Because the agonist can still displace it when its concentration rises, the antagonist produces a **parallel rightward shift** of the agonist dose-response curve with **no change in the maximum response** (it is surmountable). The size of the shift is the **dose ratio** r, the factor by which the agonist concentration must increase to give the same response. In the presence of an antagonist at concentration [B] with equilibrium dissociation constant KB, r = 1 + [B]/KB (the Schild equation). By contrast, an irreversible or non-competitive antagonist reduces the maximum response and cannot be overcome by raising the agonist dose.

blocks.caption: r = dose ratio (agonist EC50 with antagonist divided by EC50 without); [B] = antagonist concentration; KB = antagonist dissociation constant (same concentration units as [B]). Valid for simple reversible competitive antagonism.

blocks.title: Dose ratio and shifted EC50
blocks.prompt: An agonist has EC50 = 4 nM. A competitive antagonist is present at 6 nM with KB = 2 nM. Calculate the dose ratio and the new apparent EC50 of the agonist. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: New EC50 = r x original EC50 = 4 x 4 nM = 16 nM.
The curve is shifted four-fold to the right, with the same maximum. To restore the same response the agonist concentration must be increased four-fold.

blocks.answer: Dose ratio 4; apparent EC50 16 nM; maximum unchanged

blocks.markdown: **Receptor families.** Receptors fall into four main families, which differ in structure, speed of response and examples.

blocks.caption: Four main receptor families.
rows: Ligand binding opens a channel pore, changing ion flow and membrane potential
Seven-transmembrane receptor activates G proteins and second messengers (cAMP, IP3)
Ligand binding activates intrinsic or associated tyrosine kinase activity and phosphorylation cascades
Insulin receptor, growth factor receptors, cytokine receptors
Lipid-soluble ligand enters the cell and the receptor alters gene transcription
Corticosteroid, oestrogen and thyroid hormone receptors

blocks.title: Speed follows mechanism
blocks.text: The further the receptor is from a direct change in ion flow, the slower the response. This explains why corticosteroids take hours to act whereas an agonist at a ligand-gated channel acts within milliseconds.

blocks.title: Partial agonists as antagonists
blocks.text: A partial agonist with high affinity can displace a full agonist and lower the net response. Buprenorphine can therefore precipitate withdrawal in someone dependent on a full opioid agonist.

points: Agonists have affinity and efficacy (full or partial), antagonists have affinity without efficacy, and inverse agonists reduce constitutive receptor activity.
A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist dose-response curve to the right in parallel with no change in maximum; the dose ratio is 1 + [B]/KB.
Receptors comprise ligand-gated channels (milliseconds), GPCRs (seconds), kinase-linked receptors (minutes to hours) and nuclear receptors (hours to days).

questions.stem: Which description best defines a partial agonist?

options.text: A ligand that binds and activates a receptor but produces less than the maximal response even at full occupancy
A ligand that binds without activating the receptor
A ligand that reduces baseline receptor activity
A ligand that binds irreversibly to the receptor

questions.correctOptionText: A ligand that binds and activates a receptor but produces less than the maximal response even at full occupancy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: partial agonists have affinity and intermediate intrinsic efficacy.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this describes a neutral antagonist.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: this describes an inverse agonist.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: irreversibility is separate from efficacy.

questions.explanation: A partial agonist has affinity and some, but not full, intrinsic efficacy, so its maximum response is lower than that of a full agonist. In the presence of a full agonist it can act as a functional antagonist.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man dependent on methadone (a full mu opioid agonist) is given buprenorphine and develops sweating, abdominal cramps and agitation within an hour. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Buprenorphine, a high-affinity partial agonist, displaced methadone and lowered the net receptor activation
Buprenorphine is an inverse agonist at all receptors
Buprenorphine increased the intrinsic efficacy of methadone
Buprenorphine is a full agonist with higher efficacy than methadone

questions.correctOptionText: Buprenorphine, a high-affinity partial agonist, displaced methadone and lowered the net receptor activation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: displacing a full agonist with a lower-efficacy ligand reduces net signalling, producing withdrawal.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu receptors.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: a ligand does not change another's efficacy.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: a full agonist would not reduce activation.

questions.explanation: Buprenorphine binds mu receptors tightly but activates them only partially. When it replaces a full agonist the total receptor activation falls, which in a dependent patient manifests as withdrawal.

questions.stem: A ligand reduces receptor activity below the level seen with no drug present in a system with constitutive activity. How should it be classified?

options.text: Inverse agonist
Partial agonist
Full agonist
Neutral antagonist

distractorRationale.a: Correct: only an inverse agonist reduces basal activity.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: a partial agonist increases activity above baseline.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: a full agonist increases activity.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: a neutral antagonist leaves basal activity unchanged.

questions.explanation: A neutral antagonist only blocks agonists, leaving constitutive activity unchanged. An inverse agonist stabilises the inactive receptor conformation and lowers basal signalling.

questions.stem: Insulin acts on a receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity. To which receptor family does it belong?

options.text: Kinase-linked receptors
Ligand-gated ion channels
G-protein-coupled receptors
Nuclear receptors

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: ion channel receptors open pores.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: GPCRs signal through G proteins.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: nuclear receptors are intracellular transcription factors.

questions.explanation: Kinase-linked receptors phosphorylate tyrosine residues upon ligand binding, triggering signalling cascades. This family also includes growth factor receptors.

questions.stem: Why does the anti-inflammatory effect of a corticosteroid take hours to develop whereas a nicotinic receptor agonist acts within milliseconds?

options.text: Corticosteroids act through nuclear receptors that alter gene transcription, whereas nicotinic receptors are ion channels
Corticosteroids bind irreversibly to ion channels
Nicotinic receptors alter gene transcription
Corticosteroids act only at G-protein-coupled receptors

questions.correctOptionText: Corticosteroids act through nuclear receptors that alter gene transcription, whereas nicotinic receptors are ion channels

distractorRationale.a: Correct: transcription and protein synthesis take hours, channel opening takes milliseconds.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: corticosteroids act on intracellular receptors.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: the principal mechanism is nuclear.

questions.explanation: Nuclear receptors change gene expression, a process requiring transcription and translation, so the effect develops over hours. Ligand-gated channels directly alter membrane potential almost instantly.

questions.stem: A competitive antagonist is present at a concentration of 10 nM and has KB = 2 nM. Using r = 1 + [B]/KB, calculate the dose ratio.
questions.explanation: r = 1 + 10/2 = 1 + 5 = 6. The agonist concentration must be six times higher to produce the same response as without the antagonist.

questions.stem: An agonist has EC50 = 5 nM. In the presence of a competitive antagonist the dose ratio is 8. Calculate the apparent EC50 of the agonist in nM.
questions.explanation: Dose ratio is the factor by which EC50 increases, so the new EC50 = 5 x 8 = 40 nM. The curve shifts to the right in parallel and the maximum response is unchanged.

questions.stem: Compare ligand-gated ion channels, G-protein-coupled receptors, kinase-linked receptors and nuclear receptors in terms of mechanism, speed and one example of each.
markingGuide: Ligand-gated ion channels: ligand opens a pore, ion flux changes membrane potential, milliseconds; nicotinic ACh or GABA-A receptor
GPCRs: seven-transmembrane receptor activates G proteins and second messengers, seconds; beta-adrenoceptor or muscarinic receptor
Kinase-linked receptors: ligand binding activates tyrosine kinase and phosphorylation cascades, minutes to hours; insulin or growth factor receptor
Nuclear receptors: lipid-soluble ligand enters the cell, regulates gene transcription, hours to days; steroid or thyroid hormone receptor
Speed linked to mechanism; location (membrane versus intracellular)
questions.explanation: The families differ in how directly ligand binding changes cell function. The speed of response increases with the directness of the mechanism.

questions.stem: Describe the effect of a reversible competitive antagonist on an agonist dose-response curve, and contrast this with an irreversible antagonist.
markingGuide: Competitive antagonist binds the same site reversibly with no efficacy
Curve shifts in parallel to the right (higher EC50), with unchanged maximal response
Effect is surmountable by raising agonist concentration
Irreversible (or non-competitive) antagonist reduces the maximal response and cannot be overcome by increasing agonist dose
Clinical consequence: larger agonist dose may be needed with competitive antagonist; for irreversible antagonists effect persists until new receptors are synthesised
questions.explanation: A competitive antagonist reduces the proportion of receptors available to the agonist but can be outcompeted at high agonist concentration. An irreversible antagonist removes receptors from the pool, lowering the maximum.

questions.stem: True or false: a reversible competitive antagonist lowers the maximal response of the agonist.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A reversible competitive antagonist shifts the curve to the right without changing the maximum, because a high enough agonist concentration can overcome the block. A reduced maximum characterises irreversible or non-competitive antagonism.
